There is no browser on this phone to open that with.

Your log stays on this phone, and identifying a bird happens here. The app goes online for two things only: the BirdNET model, downloaded once from GitHub (about 39MB), and a bird\'s photograph from Cornell\'s image server, for a row you open, or as a bird is heard if Photo while listening is on. Those requests carry nothing you have heard or written; the servers see your internet address and which bird\'s picture was asked for. eBird and Wikipedia open in your browser only when you press them.

The microphone is open only while Birding is listening, and the sound is not kept unless you turn on Save recordings. Location is used only to weigh which birds are likely where you are, if you allow it or type a place in. The place is stored with each hearing in your log, so it goes out with a sent log or a backup; a shared hearing includes it only if you switch that on in Settings. There are no ads, no analytics and no tracking. Backups and exports go only where you choose to save them.

A fork of whoBIRD by woheller69.

BirdNET — Stefan Kahl, Connor Wood, Maximilian Eibl and Holger Klinck, of the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and Chemnitz University of Technology.

Photographs — Macaulay Library, Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Each picture belongs to its photographer. It is fetched from Cornell's server to show you the bird, kept in this app's cache, and is not licensed for any other use.
